analysis.one_liner: Makes it harder and costlier for citizens to sue water polluters in federal court.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by three House Republicans, never left committee: no hearing, no vote, dead when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the part of the Clean Water Act that lets ordinary citizens sue polluters in federal court. It would cap the attorney fees a winning citizen group can recover, bar a suit whenever a government agency has merely issued a compliance order, and add broad new defenses for dischargers. The practical effect would be to make private enforcement of water pollution laws much harder and cheaper for the companies it polices.
analysis.who_benefits: Facilities that discharge pollutants into water — factories, wastewater systems, and other permitted dischargers — gain the most. They would face less risk of being sued by citizens' groups: fee awards would be capped at amounts tied to the number of claims won or to the penalties imposed [S2][S3], a suit could not even begin once the EPA or a state issues a compliance order, which the bill defines as "diligent prosecution" for up to a year [S2][S3], and dischargers would get new affirmative defenses (act of God, war, third-party acts) plus all common-law defenses available in other federal criminal cases [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Caps what a prevailing citizen group can recover in attorney and expert fees: the award cannot exceed a share proportional to the claims actually won, cannot exceed the monetary penalties imposed, and must match local market rates [S2][S3].

Bars citizens from filing suit whenever the EPA or a state has issued a compliance order, and defines that order as 'diligent prosecution' for a full year — even though an order is a promise to fix a problem, not proof the problem is fixed [S2][S3].

Gives dischargers new affirmative defenses — act of God, act of war, third-party acts — and opens the door to every general defense available in other federal criminal cases, which defense lawyers could argue broadly [S2][S3].
Lets courts require plaintiffs seeking an injunction to post a bond, adding upfront cost to lawsuits by community groups [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People who live near polluted water and rely on citizen suits as the enforcement tool of last resort. When agencies are slow, understaffed, or persuaded by an order on paper, the citizen suit is often the only way pollution actually gets stopped; this bill would close that door earlier and make the lawsuits that survive far more expensive for the citizens who bring them [S2][S3]. Public-interest environmental law groups would bear the cost directly, since capped fees are what fund this litigation [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near polluted water; environmental law groups

drawbacks.text: Supporters' good-faith case: fee arrangements under the current law can reward lawyers who bundle many claims, settle a few, and collect outsized fees, and citizens sometimes sue over matters the government is already addressing; the bill would tie fees to actual success and prevent duplicative suits [S2][S3].

The cost an honest supporter must acknowledge: the bill counts a mere compliance order as 'diligent prosecution,' so an agency could shield a polluter from citizen suits for a year by issuing an order without any proof of actual cleanup [S2][S3].

Capping fees at the amount of monetary penalties creates a race to the bottom — the lower the penalty, the less a citizen group can recover, which prices small community groups out of court even when they win [S3].

Letting 'all general defenses... that may apply with respect to other Federal criminal offenses' apply to civil Clean Water Act liability is a sweeping change whose scope courts would have to untangle for years [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated goals — proportionate fees and no duplicate lawsuits — address real, narrow concerns. But its main mechanics go far beyond that: treating an unproven compliance order as diligent prosecution, capping fees at penalty amounts, and importing criminal defenses into civil pollution liability together would disarm the private enforcement tool that historically cleaned up water when government would not act. The savings to polluters would come directly out of communities' ability to protect their own water.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its water subcommittee, and nothing ever happened after that — no hearing, no vote — before Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Duncan Hunter introduced the bill on May 25, 2017, joined by Reps. Tom McClintock and Ken Calvert, both California Republicans [S1][S3][S4].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee [S1][S5].
The next day it was sent to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, where it sat; the action record shows no hearing, no markup, and no vote for the rest of the 115th Congress [S5].
The bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, without ever reaching the House floor [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who depend on citizen suits to force polluters to clean up are better off, because the tool survived intact; the industries the bill would have shielded gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Republicans and no Democrat cosponsored; the bill never advanced far enough to attract or reveal broader support.

industries.industry: Industrial and municipal water polluters (factories, wastewater treatment systems, other permitted dischargers)
industries.note: The bill would cut their biggest private-enforcement risks: capped fee exposure, a suit bar triggered by any compliance order, and new affirmative defenses. The gain comes directly at the expense of communities living with the pollution.
Citizen-suit fee recovery is what makes their enforcement work financially possible; the bill's fee caps, bond requirements, and diligent-prosecution bar would shrink or end much of that litigation.
